title: Hardening a Fresh Ubuntu Server
excerpt: A compact baseline for patching, firewall rules, SSH hygiene, logs, and package inventory.
body: Start every server build with a repeatable baseline. Update packages, remove services you do not need, and keep a note of what changed.
Use firewall defaults before opening ports. SSH should prefer keys, limited users, and clear logging so suspicious access attempts are visible early.
Finish by taking a package inventory and recording the commands in the ticket or change log.
commands: sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade
sudo ufw default deny incoming && sudo ufw allow OpenSSH && sudo ufw enable

title: Reading Linux Logs Like a Defender
excerpt: A simple workflow for finding warning patterns in systemd, auth, kernel, and web service logs.
body: Good log review starts with a small question. Look for failed authentications, new services, privilege changes, and unexpected network listeners.
Keep the first pass narrow. Pull warnings from the last hour, expand the time window only when the first signal looks meaningful, and compare with known maintenance windows.
Turn useful searches into saved snippets so the same review can be repeated by another analyst.

title: Building an AppSec Scan Checklist
excerpt: Combine dependency, secret, static analysis, and dynamic checks before every public release.
body: An AppSec checklist works best when it is boring, consistent, and attached to the release workflow. Start with dependency and secret checks because they are fast and easy to automate.
Add static analysis for code patterns and container scanning for runtime images. Dynamic testing belongs in a controlled staging environment with written authorization.
Keep every finding tied to an owner, a fix version, and a retest note.

title: Incident Triage in the First Hour
excerpt: A calm first-hour routine for scoping, preserving evidence, and deciding what must be contained.
body: The first hour is about clarity, not heroics. Preserve volatile evidence, write down who noticed what, and identify the business systems that may be affected.
Separate facts from guesses. Track timestamps in one place and keep containment actions small enough to explain later.
When evidence points to active compromise, prioritize account control, exposed service reduction, and forensic capture before broad rebuild work.

title: A Practical Web Vulnerability Assessment Flow
excerpt: A start-to-finish assessment path for scope, mapping, passive scanning, validation, evidence, and reporting.
body: A useful vulnerability assessment begins before tools run. Confirm written authorization, approved targets, time window, rate limits, accounts, and exclusions.
Map the application manually first. Record roles, key workflows, API endpoints, forms, file uploads, redirects, cookies, and security headers before trusting scanner output.

Run passive and low-risk automated checks in an approved window, then manually validate only the findings that matter. A good report explains impact, evidence, and remediation in language an owner can act on.

title: Web Hacking Playbook for Legal Labs
excerpt: What to check in authentication, access control, APIs, input validation, configuration, and reporting.
body: Treat web testing like a controlled experiment. For every suspected bug, capture the starting account, exact request, exact response, expected behavior, and business impact.
Access control testing is usually the highest-value area. Build a role matrix, then compare what each user can see and change across accounts, organizations, tenants, and admin functions.
Input validation testing should avoid destructive payloads. Start with scanner findings, safe test cases, and logs from the staging environment so the proof is clear without harming data.

title: Writing Findings That Actually Get Fixed
excerpt: A clean finding template for severity, affected asset, evidence, impact, remediation, and retest.
body: A finding is not just a bug title. It should name the affected asset, explain who can trigger the issue, show the evidence, and describe what could happen in realistic business terms.
Severity should combine impact and likelihood. Tool output is a starting point, not the final risk rating.
Close the loop with remediation and retest steps. A developer should understand the control that failed and the exact condition that proves it is fixed.
commands: Title: Broken access control exposes another user's invoice
Evidence: request ID, affected endpoint, two test accounts, timestamp
Fix: enforce server-side ownership checks before returning object data
